passage: The first time I volunteered at the community kitchen near the railway colony, I arrived with a plan to reorganise everything. I'd read about kitchens abroad and had ideas. Vidya-akka, who had run it for eleven years, let me talk for five minutes. Then she handed me an apron and said, 'Chop onions today, Lakshmi. Talk to people tomorrow.' I was a bit offended. But over the next month I learned why they served lunch at two, not twelve: most of the people came after morning shifts. My brilliant plans would have broken things. Now I help with the accounts, which is actually useful. I still catch myself wanting to be thanked. I'm trying to notice that and just show up.

qa.q: How long had Vidya-akka run the community kitchen?
qa.a: She had run it for eleven years.

qa.q: What does Lakshmi admit about wanting to be thanked?
qa.a: Lakshmi admits still wanting praise at times, which shows awareness of that ego.

qa.q: What made Vidya-akka's instruction wise?
qa.a: It made Lakshmi learn how the kitchen actually worked before trying to change it.

qa.q: How might the people eating at the kitchen see volunteers like early Lakshmi?
qa.a: They might see eager outsiders who don't understand their routines and could accidentally make things harder.

grounding: Shows a young volunteer learning to listen and serve without assuming they know best.

passage:
Coordinator's note, Aditi, evening literacy classes, Saturday.

Jasleen, a college student, joined us three weeks ago. On her first evening she spoke slowly and loudly to the women in class, as if they were children, and took photos of them for her college project without asking. I spoke to her privately. She went pink and apologised, and deleted the photos in front of me. Since then she has changed noticeably. She now asks the learners what they want to read. Last week one woman wanted to read her bus route signs, so Jasleen made cards with the stop names. She told me she'd stopped thinking of it as 'helping' and more as working alongside them. I have asked her to help plan next month's sessions.

qa.q: What did one woman want to read?
qa.a: She wanted to read her bus route signs.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel when Aditi spoke to her, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and sorry; she went pink, apologised and deleted the photos.

qa.q: What change in Jasleen's approach made her more useful?
qa.a: She began asking learners what they wanted, such as making bus stop cards, instead of deciding for them.

qa.q: How might the women in class have felt on Jasleen's first evening?
qa.a: They may have felt talked down to and uncomfortable being photographed without being asked.

grounding: Shows an adult coordinator noting a young volunteer move from a condescending approach to working alongside learners.

passage:
Wednesday

Clean-up drive at the lake today. Lavanya and I did three hours. I wanted to post a photo of us with the rubbish bags, and I almost did. Then I saw the fishermen's families who live there picking up plastic every morning without anyone clicking photos. I felt a bit fake. 😕

Asked one of the older men what would actually help. He said the drain from the market dumps into the lake every week and nobody listens to them. That's not something a Sunday selfie fixes.

Lavanya knows someone at the ward office. We're going to go with him next week and just listen, not take over. Maybe carry the letter he's already written.

Didn't post the photo. Felt better, weirdly.
— Imran

qa.q: Where did Imran and Lavanya do the clean-up drive?
qa.a: They did it at the lake.

qa.q: How did Imran feel about posting the photo, and why?
qa.a: Imran felt uncomfortable and a bit fake after seeing the local families quietly pick up plastic every morning, so the post seemed more about looking good than helping.

qa.q: What makes Imran's new plan more useful than the photo?
qa.a: Supporting the older man's existing effort with the ward office tackles the real cause, the market drain, while letting him lead.

qa.q: How might the fishermen's families feel about volunteers who only come for photos?
qa.a: They might feel ignored or used, since their daily work and real problems stay invisible.

grounding: Shows a young volunteer questioning their own motives and choosing to support locals' own efforts instead of seeking credit.

passage:
Sachin: posted the pics from today's session! the kids were so cute, they loved me 😄
Chandrika: glad it went well. can you take down the ones with their faces though? we need parents' consent for that
Sachin: oh. sorry, didn't think
Chandrika: it's ok, everyone does it once
Sachin: I also wrote 'giving these poor kids a chance' in the caption. is that bad
Chandrika: honestly? a bit. they're not waiting to be rescued. they teach us stuff too. Meena explained the fractions game better than I could
Sachin: true, she was sharper than me today
Sachin: ok deleted. what else should I change
Chandrika: come regularly, same day each week. that matters more than big gestures. and ask the kids what they want to learn
Sachin: will do. Saturday 4 pm is mine now
Chandrika: 🙏

qa.q: What did Chandrika ask Sachin to take down?
qa.a: The pictures showing the children's faces, since they need parents' consent.

qa.q: What does Sachin's 'is that bad' suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He was starting to doubt his caption and genuinely wanted to learn rather than defend himself.

qa.q: What makes Chandrika's advice good for volunteering?
qa.a: Showing up regularly and asking the children what they want keeps the focus on them instead of on the volunteer's image.

qa.q: How might the children see a caption calling them 'poor kids'?
qa.a: As making them objects of pity rather than capable learners like Meena.

grounding: A chat shows a volunteer coordinator steering a new volunteer away from a saviour mindset towards steady, respectful service.

passage: Parveen arrived in the village near Barmer with a suitcase of donated storybooks and a plan: a reading corner for girls in the panchayat hall. On the first day, only three girls came. Ujjwal, the local schoolteacher who had invited her volunteer group, didn't say much. That evening, sitting on his doorstep, she asked why. 'The girls fetch water between four and six,' he said. 'Your timing is their work time.' Parveen felt her cheeks burn. She had planned from her college room, not from here. The next morning she went to the women at the well and asked when the girls were free. Early morning, they said, and Sundays. She moved the corner and asked two older girls to choose which books went on the shelf. By the second week the hall was full, and it no longer felt like her project.

qa.q: What did Parveen bring to the village?
qa.a: A suitcase of donated storybooks.

qa.q: Why did Parveen's cheeks burn when Ujjwal explained the timing?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, realising she had planned from her college room without learning about the girls' daily lives.

qa.q: What changed Parveen's project for the better?
qa.a: Asking the women when the girls were free and letting older girls choose the books made the corner fit the community.

qa.q: How might the older girls feel being asked to choose the books?
qa.a: Trusted and involved, so the reading corner feels like theirs rather than an outsider's.

grounding: Shows a young volunteer learning to listen to a village community and let go of ownership of her project.
